hints: Focus on what actually gets hot here, the water in the copper can absorbs the heat released by the burning fuel.
Work out two separate numbers first, the heat gained by the water using $q = mc\Delta T$, and the moles of butan-1-ol actually burned from the loss in mass of the burner.
Connect them with enthalpy per mole as heat released divided by moles burned, remembering combustion is exothermic so the sign is negative and the answer must be in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
**Find the heat gained by the water**

Think of the water as a heat collector. Its mass is $175 \text{ cm}^3 \times 1.00 \text{ g cm}^{-3} = 175 \text{ g}$ and its rise is $41.1 - 17.6 = 23.5 ^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Chemical calculation rule:
$$q = mc\Delta T = 175 \times 4.18 \times 23.5 = 17190 \text{ J} \approx 17.2 \text{ kJ}$$

**Find the moles of butan-1-ol burned**

The burner gets lighter because fuel has burned away. Mass burned is initial minus final.

Chemical calculation rule:
$$m(\text{fuel}) = 58.34 - 57.85 = 0.49 \text{ g}$$
$$n = \frac{m}{M_r} = \frac{0.49}{74} = 0.00662 \text{ mol}$$

**Convert heat to molar enthalpy of combustion**

That $17.2 \text{ kJ}$ came from only $0.00662 \text{ mol}$. For one mole, divide heat by moles. Combustion gives out heat, so $\Delta H_c$ is negative.

Chemical calculation rule:
$$\Delta H_c = -\frac{q}{n} = -\frac{17.190}{0.00662} \approx -2600 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**Sense check the size**

Alcohol combustions are very exothermic, typically thousands of $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. A value of only tens of $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ or only hundreds of $\text{J mol}^{-1}$ is far too small, which helps you spot the correct magnitude.

options.A: Far too small in both number and units. A molar enthalpy of combustion of about $100 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$ is impossible for an alcohol, it should be thousands of $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. This comes from muddling the $q = mc\Delta T$ step with the per-mole step and leaving the answer in $\text{J}$ instead of $\text{kJ}$.
options.B: This is the heat absorbed by the water, $17.2 \text{ kJ}$, not the molar enthalpy. The trap is to stop after $q = mc\Delta T$ and forget to divide by the moles of butan-1-ol burned ($0.49 \text{ g} / 74$).
options.C: Correct. Water heat $q = 175 \times 4.18 \times 23.5 \approx 17.2 \text{ kJ}$ divided by moles burned $0.49/74 \approx 0.00662 \text{ mol}$ gives about $2600 \text{ kJ}$ per mole, negative because combustion is exothermic.
options.D: Too negative by almost a factor of two. This is the classic temperature trap of using the final temperature $41.1 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ as $\Delta T$ instead of the rise $41.1 - 17.6 = 23.5 ^{\circ}\text{C}$, giving $q \approx 30.1 \text{ kJ}$ and about $-4540 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
